The question is whether capability-versioned, tenant-local caching can reduce invalidation costs while preserving release authorization and the median-overhead bound. It does not select unconditional recomputation as the answer.
Can a join result remain mathematically the same across versions while its use for declassification changes?

Conceptually, yes. The combination of labels and the authority to release information are distinct questions. A cached computation might produce the same label result in two contexts, yet a release permissible under one authorization state might not be permissible under another. A design would need to avoid treating an unchanged cached computation as evidence that authorization is unchanged.
Would a tenant-local cache alone prevent an authorization problem caused by revocation within that tenant?

No. Tenant-locality addresses cross-tenant reuse. Revocation can change what is authorized within the same tenant, so a cache confined to that tenant can still contain a result associated with an earlier capability state. The proposed versioning is meant to address that separate dimension, but whether it succeeds remains the question.
When we say “reduce invalidation costs,” are we promising fewer invalidations or faster ones?

Neither specific mechanism is promised. The question asks whether this cache arrangement can reduce invalidation costs; it does not define a count of invalidations, a time per invalidation, or a particular invalidation strategy. An evaluation would need a consistent meaning for cost before concluding that it was reduced.
Could reducing invalidation work merely move the cost to version checks or retained cache entries?

Yes, that is why the cost question cannot be answered by counting invalidations alone. Version-sensitive reuse may impose other work or resource use. What matters for the performance condition is the resulting median workflow latency overhead, while the security condition still requires that no revoked release be admitted. The node gives no measurements of either effect.
Does “without exceeding 15% median overhead” mean each workflow must have overhead of at most 15%?

No. It concerns median overhead, not a per-workflow ceiling. The broader runtime target is median workflow latency overhead below 15% relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement. Strictly speaking, a median of exactly 15% would not satisfy “below 15%,” even though it would not exceed 15%; a careful assessment should retain the stricter stated goal.
Could an improvement in median overhead justify allowing a revoked release in a rare case?

No. The question asks for reduced invalidation costs *without* admitting revoked releases and without breaching the overhead condition. Performance is not permission to extend declassification beyond the tenant’s valid authorization. A favorable median would answer only the cost part.
What would have to be true for an old join-cache entry to be harmless after a capability is revoked?

It would have to be unable to authorize or otherwise enable a release that revocation disallows. That could mean its reuse is excluded when the relevant authorization state differs, or that any reuse is confined to computations independent of that authority. Those are conceptual conditions, not a selected implementation. They would also have to hold when work is retried and interleaved with other tenants’ work.
Does keeping join caches tenant-local answer the information-flow question for shared caches generally?

No. It describes the scope of the proposed *label-join cache*. It does not by itself settle every flow through the runtime’s other shared caches, concurrent execution, or retry scheduling. The immediate question is whether this particular arrangement reduces invalidation costs without compromising release authorization or the median-overhead condition.
How could we assess the security and performance sides without confusing them?

Assess whether a revoked capability can still lead to a release through a cached join or a retry, and separately measure the resulting median workflow latency overhead against identical executions without information-flow enforcement. To answer the cost part, compare invalidation costs on a consistent basis. A finding about one measure should not be presented as a result for the others; this question supplies none of those findings.
Would observing no revoked releases in a finite set of cases prove that versioned caching is safe for all interleavings?

No. Such an observation would be limited to the cases examined. A general claim would also have to account for the applicable authorization states and the ways cache access, revocation, and retries can interleave. The current node poses that as an open question, not as a completed evaluation or proof.
Can you restate the open question precisely?

Can tenant-local label-join caches keyed or otherwise distinguished by capability version lower invalidation costs while ensuring that revoked release authority is never used to permit a disclosure, and still keep median workflow latency overhead below the runtime’s 15% target relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement? The proposed benefits and safeguards remain to be established.

Here is the hypothesis: partitions had zero mismatches at 16.8% median overhead; tenant-local epoch-keyed joins should avoid invalidations, save at least 1.9 percentage points, and block revocation leaks. Can you separate the observation from the prediction?

The observation is that the partition configuration had zero reported low-trace mismatches at 16.8% median overhead. The prediction is that tenant-local epoch-keyed label joins will avoid join-cache invalidations, reduce median overhead by at least 1.9 percentage points, and prevent revoked release authority from leaking information. None of those predicted effects is a new measured result.
Why is the proposed saving stated as at least 1.9 points?

Starting from 16.8% median overhead, a reduction of 1.9 percentage points would yield 14.9% on a comparable overhead measure. That is below the runtime’s strict 15% target. “At least” means the hypothesis predicts a saving of 1.9 percentage points or more; it does not report that saving as observed.
Are percentage points and percent interchangeable in that calculation?
No. Subtracting 1.9 percentage points from 16.8% gives 14.9%. A reduction of 1.9% of 16.8% would be a different, smaller change. The hypothesis specifically says to save at least 1.9 points.
Does that arithmetic guarantee the new median will be below 15%?

Only conditionally: if the measured median overhead is comparable to the stated 16.8% figure and the proposed change actually saves at least 1.9 percentage points, the resulting figure would be no more than 14.9%. The arithmetic explains the target; it cannot establish that the optimization works or that its other effects leave the measured median unchanged.
What does “tenant-local epoch-keyed joins” mean at the level this hypothesis specifies?

It proposes keeping cached label-join results within a tenant’s context and distinguishing their reuse by an epoch associated with the relevant authorization state. The intent is to avoid treating a result from one state as valid in another. The hypothesis does not specify an epoch representation, when epochs change, or the exact form of a cache key.
How could epoch-keying avoid invalidations without keeping stale authority usable?

The proposed idea is to make an entry associated with an earlier epoch unavailable for authorization-sensitive reuse in a later epoch, rather than relying on invalidating that entry when the state changes. That could avoid some invalidation work while preventing a stale result from being treated as current. It is a rationale for the hypothesis, not evidence that every access or retry observes the right epoch.
Does “avoid invalidations” mean no cache anywhere in the runtime would ever invalidate an entry?

No. The hypothesis concerns tenant-local epoch-keyed label joins and the invalidation costs motivating that change. It should not be stretched into a claim that all caches or all kinds of invalidation disappear. Even for the join cache, avoiding invalidations is still a predicted effect to evaluate.
What does tenant-locality contribute if epochs already distinguish authorization states?

They distinguish different things. Tenant-locality confines join-result reuse to the relevant tenant context; epoch-keying distinguishes states within that context. An epoch distinction alone would not, by its name, establish that results are kept separate between tenants. Conversely, tenant-locality alone would not distinguish an earlier authorization state from a later one within a tenant.
What exactly is a revocation leak in this hypothesis?

It is a disclosure that relies on release authority after that authority has been revoked. The proposed join caching must not let a result associated with an earlier epoch effectively admit such a release. “Block revocation leaks” is a security prediction here, not a finding that any particular revoked release was attempted or prevented.
If an old entry stays in memory after revocation, has the hypothesis already failed?

Not merely because the entry remains stored. The security question is whether it can be used to permit a release that revocation disallows. Avoiding invalidation might leave old entries present but unusable for authorization-sensitive work in a different epoch. Whether the actual design maintains that boundary, including on retries, remains to be established.
Could the cached join still be correct as a label calculation while its use for a release is wrong?

Yes. Reusing a label-combination result and authorizing declassification are distinct matters. Even if the computed join is unchanged, a revoked release must not be admitted on the strength of earlier authority. The hypothesis needs both faithful reuse of label joins and enforcement of the current release boundary.
How do concurrent retries put pressure on the epoch idea?

A retry may revisit work associated with an earlier authorization context while other work continues. The proposed protection would have to ensure that revisiting that work does not turn an earlier epoch’s cached result into valid authority after revocation. The hypothesis does not specify how a retry obtains or checks its epoch, so that remains a question for the design rather than an established safeguard.
Would a retry carrying its original label settle that issue?

Not by itself. Preserving a label keeps information-flow context with retried work, but it does not automatically decide whether a release capability is still usable after revocation. Epoch-keyed joins are proposed to address reuse across authorization states; the retry path still has to respect that distinction.
Does the earlier zero-mismatch observation mean we can assume this change preserves zero mismatches?

No. The zero-mismatch figure describes the observed partition configuration at 16.8% median overhead. Changing join-cache behavior introduces a new proposition to assess. The hypothesis predicts blocked revocation leaks and lower cost, but it does not report a low-trace comparison after introducing tenant-local epoch-keyed joins.
Is blocking revocation leaks sufficient by itself to establish the whole noninterference goal?

No. It addresses one release-authorization concern. The broader goal also covers information-flow isolation under concurrent execution and retries, including shared-cache effects, with only tenant-authorized declassification excepted. Preventing revoked releases would be important, but this hypothesis alone is neither a complete proof of that goal nor a measurement of every relevant trace.
Could versioning the join results cause overhead elsewhere even if it avoids invalidation work?

It could. Distinguishing and using epochs may involve work of its own, and the hypothesis supplies no component-level cost measurements. That is why the proposed saving must be checked as a change in median workflow latency overhead, rather than inferred solely from fewer invalidations.
How should the median overhead comparison be read?

The 16.8% is the stated median overhead for partitions. The hypothesized improvement is at least 1.9 percentage points on the median workflow latency overhead measure, whose reference is identical executions without information-flow enforcement. That would place a comparable median at or below 14.9%, but the hypothesis gives no measured overhead for the epoch-keyed design.
Could we accept 15.0% because the question was phrased as not exceeding 15%?

The runtime’s stated target is strictly below 15% median overhead. A measured 15.0% would not meet that target. The hypothesis’s at-least-1.9-point saving from 16.8% is framed to reach 14.9% or less if it holds on a comparable basis.
What would need to be evaluated separately to judge this hypothesis?

First, whether tenant-local epoch-keyed joins actually avoid the relevant invalidations and produce a saving of at least 1.9 percentage points in median workflow latency overhead. Second, whether revoked release authority remains unusable through cached joins and concurrent retries. Low-trace behavior should also remain within the authorized-release exception rather than being inferred from the overhead result. No such evaluation outcome is stated here.
Can you give me a precise restatement that preserves both the observed starting point and the uncertainty?

Partitions had zero reported low-trace mismatches at 16.8% median overhead. The hypothesis is that tenant-local epoch-keyed label joins can avoid join-cache invalidations, lower that comparable median overhead by at least 1.9 percentage points, and block disclosures based on revoked release authority. The predicted cost and security effects remain unverified.

Let’s implement tenant-local epoch-keyed join caches, replay revocation races in FlowPair-10k-Release v1, and measure unauthorized releases, trace mismatches, and median overhead. What is this activity meant to establish?

It is an evaluation activity, not an established result. The implementation introduces tenant-local epoch-keyed caching for label joins. The FlowPair-10k-Release v1 runs then examine how that caching behaves when revocation and retried work can interact. The three measurements address distinct questions: whether any release occurs without valid authorization, whether compared low traces mismatch after accounting for authorized releases, and what median workflow latency overhead the implementation incurs.
What is the cache meant to reuse?

It is a cache of label-join results: results of combining information-flow labels. Calling it tenant-local means reuse is confined to the relevant tenant context; calling it epoch-keyed means the relevant epoch distinguishes cached results. The activity does not specify a key format, an epoch representation, or the cache’s storage arrangement.
Why does the epoch matter when a capability is revoked?

Revocation can change which release authority is applicable. An epoch-keyed result is intended to distinguish work associated with different authorization states so that an older cached result cannot simply be treated as current authority. That is the concern the activity is designed to examine. Implementing an epoch in a key does not, by itself, demonstrate that every release and retry respects revocation.
Does this activity say how an epoch advances on revocation?

No. It calls for implementing tenant-local epoch-keyed join caches and replaying revocation races, but does not define the epoch-transition mechanism. Any claim that a particular transition rule is implemented or correct would add a detail not stated here.
What does it mean to replay a revocation race?

Conceptually, it means exercising cases in which revocation and work that might use release authority occur close enough in the execution order for that order to matter. Retried work is particularly relevant because it may revisit an earlier authorization context. The activity says to replay such races in FlowPair-10k-Release v1; it does not specify the individual schedules, how many are replayed, or their outcomes.
Is the aim to reject every release whenever revocation and a retry overlap?

That is not specified. The concern is whether a release is authorized under the applicable capability state, not a blanket prohibition based solely on overlap. The activity must distinguish a release within valid authorization from one admitted on the strength of revoked authority. It does not prescribe a precise rule for ordering a release against revocation.
If a join result is still stored after revocation, should it count as an unauthorized release?

No. A stored join result is not itself a declassification event. The relevant question is whether using that result can help permit a disclosure that revocation disallows. The unauthorized-release measurement concerns actual releases outside valid authorization, rather than the mere presence of an old cache entry.
Could the join result itself be correct but still be unsafe to reuse?

Yes, conceptually. A label-combination result and permission to declassify are different things. A cached calculation could remain a faithful calculation while its use in a later authorization context is inappropriate. The revocation-race runs are meant to examine that distinction without presuming that epoch-keying has already handled it correctly.
Does tenant-locality alone keep a revoked release from being admitted?

No. Tenant-locality limits reuse across tenant contexts; a revocation can matter within the same tenant. Epoch-sensitive reuse is the proposed additional distinction. Whether the combined implementation prevents unauthorized releases during races is one of the measurements requested, not a conclusion of the activity statement.
What should the unauthorized-release count capture?

It should capture releases that occur without the authorization required for them, including any release improperly admitted using revoked authority in the races being evaluated. An attempted use of a capability is not automatically an actual release. The activity provides no count, so we cannot say whether any such release is observed.
Is the trace-mismatch count just another name for the unauthorized-release count?

No. A trace mismatch is a difference in compared low-visible behavior outside what authorized releases allow; an unauthorized release is a disclosure without the necessary authorization. They can be related, but one measurement cannot be substituted for the other. The activity explicitly requests both.
How do authorized releases affect the trace comparison?

The comparison should account for releases that are actually authorized, rather than counting every permitted disclosure as an impermissible low-trace difference. It must not normalize away a purported release that relied on revoked authority, nor an unrelated low-visible difference. FlowPair-10k-Release v1 is the named setting for this evaluation, but this node does not state a trace-comparison result.
If a revocation race produces no unauthorized release, could there still be a trace mismatch?

Yes, as a matter of what the two measurements ask. Cache activity or retried work might affect low-visible behavior without producing a declassification event. Whether that occurs in these runs is unknown. That is why measuring unauthorized releases alone would not answer the entire trace-isolation question.
Conversely, can we infer authorization solely because the low traces match?

No. Trace comparison and release authorization need separate examination. A matching comparison under its chosen observations would not by itself show that every release was authorized, especially if the authorization check were assumed rather than examined. The activity calls for an unauthorized-release measurement as well.
Does replaying races in FlowPair-10k-Release v1 amount to a proof across every concurrent execution?

No. Replaying cases in the named evaluation can provide evidence about the cases examined. The activity does not claim exhaustive coverage of all possible revocations, retries, cache accesses, or interleavings, and it does not state that a formal noninterference proof has been completed.
What should the median-overhead figure include conceptually?

It is a measure of median workflow latency overhead for the evaluated enforcement, not merely the time taken by one join-cache lookup or one revocation check. The runtime’s performance comparison is against identical executions without information-flow enforcement. This activity requests a measurement but reports no percentage, so it cannot yet establish whether the below-15% target is met.
Would avoiding an invalidation automatically mean lower median overhead?

No. Epoch-keyed reuse may alter work elsewhere, so a reduction in invalidation work would not, on its own, determine the median workflow latency. The activity asks for an overhead measurement rather than assuming that a proposed cache change produces a net improvement.
Does the activity explicitly measure how many invalidations were avoided?

No. Its stated measurements are unauthorized releases, trace mismatches, and median overhead. The implementation is motivated by the question of join-cache invalidation costs, but this activity does not name a separate invalidation count or provide an invalidation-cost result.
If the median is below the target but a revoked release is admitted, has the activity succeeded overall?

A favorable median would address only the performance measure. It would not make a release based on revoked authority authorized, nor would it erase a trace mismatch. The three requested measurements should be reported separately so that performance cannot stand in for isolation or release safety.
And if neither security measure finds a problem, can we claim every future retry is safe?

No. Zero observed unauthorized releases or trace mismatches, if that were the result, would describe the evaluated cases under the comparison used. The activity has not supplied such a result, and even a finite zero count would not establish a universal guarantee for all future concurrent retries and revocation races.
Can you give me a concise, prospective statement of the activity?

Implement tenant-local epoch-keyed label-join caches, replay revocation races in FlowPair-10k-Release v1, and measure unauthorized releases, low-trace mismatches, and median workflow latency overhead. Use those measurements to evaluate release safety, observable isolation, and cost without presuming any outcome.
What did FlowPair-10k-Release v1 find when it replayed revocation races?

It found 2 revoked-capability releases in 10,000 revocation races, with 14.4% median workflow latency overhead. The overhead figure is below the 15% median target, but the two releases are a separate authorization concern; favorable latency does not make them authorized.
What exactly does “2 revoked-capability releases” count?

It counts two observed releases involving revoked capabilities across the 10,000 revocation races. It is a release count, not a stated count of distinct capabilities or affected tenants. The finding also does not say whether the two releases occurred in separate races.
Can I describe those releases as attempts that were rejected?
No. The finding says releases occurred; it does not merely report attempted uses of revoked capabilities. Recasting them as rejected attempts would change the reported result.
Why does revocation make those releases significant?

A revoked capability should not supply authority for a release that depends on it. The reported events show that, in these revocation races, two releases occurred with revoked-capability authority. The finding does not provide the individual authorizations or event sequences, so it supports that observation without a more detailed account of how each release was admitted.
Does the finding tell us which cache lookup let a revoked capability through?

No. The activity involved tenant-local epoch-keyed join caches, but the evidence does not identify a particular lookup, invalidation, epoch transition, or retry as the cause of either release. It would be premature to assign a specific implementation fault from this result alone.
Could we say epoch-keying eliminated join-cache invalidations because the median overhead is 14.4%?

No. The result reports a median overhead and two revoked-capability releases; it does not report an invalidation count or show that invalidations were eliminated. A latency figure cannot establish which internal work was avoided.
How should I interpret the 14.4% figure?

It is median workflow latency overhead for the reported FlowPair-10k-Release v1 evaluation, measured relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement. It is not the latency cost of either revoked-capability release, nor the overhead of each individual workflow.
Is 14.4% strictly below the performance target?

Yes. Numerically, 14.4% is below the goal of 15% median workflow latency overhead. That answers the median-overhead comparison for the reported run; it does not resolve the authorization concern raised by the two releases.
Can the 14.4% median tell us whether either of those releases happened in a fast or slow workflow?

No. The evidence gives no per-case latency measurements or link between the two release events and individual workflow latencies. A median summarizes the overall measured latency overhead and cannot locate either event within the latency distribution.
What if someone says that two out of 10,000 is small enough to ignore?

That would turn an observed authorization failure into a permitted exception without support. The isolation goal excepts tenant-authorized declassification, not releases merely because they are infrequent. The reported count is two revoked-capability releases in 10,000 races; the performance figure does not change what the release count means.
Is the result saying there were two low-trace mismatches as well?

No low-trace mismatch count is stated in this finding. The activity called for measuring trace mismatches, but this evidence reports revoked-capability releases and median overhead only. We cannot substitute the release count for a trace-mismatch count or infer that the traces matched.
Could a revoked-capability release be normalized away as an authorized declassification?

It should not be treated as authorized solely because it involved a capability. Release normalization concerns disclosures within valid tenant authorization. The finding calls these revoked-capability releases; it does not establish a separate authorization that would permit them. Nor does it supply individual traces from which to state a trace-comparison outcome.
Does this tell us that every retry involving revocation admits a release?
No. The evidence reports two releases across 10,000 revocation races. It does not say that every race produced a release, or characterize every possible retry and revocation ordering.
Does it prove every other race was safe in every respect?

No. The absence of additional reported revoked-capability releases is not a complete account of every other behavior in those races. In particular, this finding supplies no trace-mismatch result or exhaustive description of the cases.
Can we infer that the same revoked capability was used twice?
No. The result does not identify the capabilities involved. The two releases could not be assigned to the same or different capabilities from the information given.
Does this evidence establish a general rate of revoked releases for the runtime?

It establishes the observed count in this evaluation: 2 revoked-capability releases in 10,000 revocation races. Turning that ratio into a guaranteed rate for other workloads or all possible concurrent executions would go beyond the finding.
What can we conclude about the relationship between the security and latency observations?

They coexist in this run: the reported median overhead was 14.4%, and two revoked-capability releases were observed. The result does not say that lower overhead caused the releases, or that preventing them would necessarily change the median. It does show why the performance and release-authorization outcomes must be reported separately.
Does the result tell us what to change in the epoch-keyed cache?

No specific change is given. The two releases identify behavior that needs explanation before one could claim revoked authority is blocked, but the finding does not choose a remedy or identify a faulty cache or capability operation.
How can I report this accurately without implying a completed diagnosis or a trace result?

FlowPair-10k-Release v1 observed 2 revoked-capability releases in 10,000 revocation races with 14.4% median workflow latency overhead. The finding does not identify the cause of those releases or provide a low-trace mismatch count.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: tenant-local epoch-keyed joins plus atomic revocation-epoch validation at release commit eliminate revoked releases while maintaining median overhead below 15%. How do the two parts work together conceptually?

Tenant-local epoch-keyed joins are proposed to make cached label-join results specific to a tenant and an epoch. Atomic revocation-epoch validation at release commit is proposed as the decisive check that the release still has valid authority when it takes effect. The hypothesis is that combining them prevents releases based on revoked authority without pushing median workflow latency overhead to 15% or higher. Neither outcome is established just by stating the hypothesis.
Why isn't keying the join cache by epoch enough on its own?

An epoch-keyed lookup can distinguish cached results associated with different epochs, but a release may occur after earlier processing. The proposed commit-time validation addresses whether the authority is still valid at the point of release. A cached label computation should not be mistaken for proof that a capability remains usable at that later point.
What does “atomic” mean in this hypothesis?

It means the revocation-epoch validation and the decision to commit the release must behave as one indivisible authorization step with respect to a competing revocation. The intended property is that a release cannot pass a check under one epoch and then commit under a different, revoked state without that change being accounted for. The hypothesis does not prescribe a particular synchronization or storage mechanism.
Is the atomic check supposed to happen when the join is calculated?

No. The hypothesis specifically places atomic revocation-epoch validation at *release commit*. A join may have been calculated earlier and reused, but that earlier calculation is not a substitute for checking revocation at the moment the disclosure is committed.
How does that matter when an asynchronous retry resumes work?

A retry might revisit work whose cached join or release context originated earlier. Under the proposed approach, that earlier context would not, by itself, authorize a release when the retry reaches commit. The release would still have to pass the atomic revocation-epoch validation. Whether an implementation actually provides that behavior under all retry interleavings remains to be shown.
Does a retry have to recompute every label join after revocation?

The hypothesis does not require or rule out recomputing every join. Epoch-keying is meant to distinguish when a cached result can be reused, while commit-time validation governs whether release authority is current. The exact rules for retaining, selecting, or recomputing cached joins are not specified here.
Could an old join-cache entry stay stored after its epoch is no longer current?

Possibly. Its continued storage is different from its eligibility for reuse or its ability to authorize a release. The security prediction requires that an entry associated with an earlier epoch cannot enable a release after the relevant authority has been revoked. The hypothesis does not specify an eviction or cleanup policy for old entries.
What precisely is meant by eliminating revoked releases?

It means preventing a disclosure from being committed on the basis of capability authority that has been revoked. The claim concerns releases, not a promise that every internal cache entry disappears immediately or that all work associated with an older epoch stops. It is a predicted security property, not a reported count of observed releases.
If revocation and release commit happen concurrently, what must the validation establish?

The two operations need an unambiguous authorization relationship: the release must be checked against the revocation epoch applicable to its commit, rather than relying on a stale check performed before a concurrent change. Atomicity is intended to prevent a gap between validation and commitment from admitting revoked authority. The hypothesis does not define the exact rule for ordering a concurrent revocation and release; that rule would need to be specified to assess the claim.
Does this mean every release racing with revocation must be rejected?

No such blanket rule is stated. The requirement is to avoid releases based on revoked authority. A precise design must define when revocation takes effect relative to a release commit, then ensure the validation and commit respect that definition. Merely overlapping in time does not, by itself, settle whether a particular release is authorized.
Would successful epoch validation authorize release to any audience?

No. Checking that authority has not been revoked addresses revocation; it does not expand the capability's permitted audience or any other limit on tenant-authorized declassification. The hypothesis adds a safeguard at release commit, not blanket permission to disclose wherever the information might be sent.
Can an atomic check replace the requirement that the tenant authorize the release in the first place?

No. Validation of a revocation epoch is meaningful only alongside the underlying authorization for that release. An unrevoked epoch does not create tenant consent, and a cached join does not create it either. The proposed combination is intended to stop revoked releases while retaining the distinction between authorized and unauthorized declassification.
Does tenant-locality play a role beyond performance?

Yes. Tenant-locality confines the proposed join-cache reuse to a tenant context, so a join result is not treated as though it were independent of the tenant whose information-flow constraints it represents. Epoch-keying addresses a different distinction: changes in the relevant authority state within that context. Neither boundary alone establishes that commit-time release validation is correct.
Could the commit-time check make the cache optimization pointless?

That is an open performance question. The intended division of work is to reuse eligible label-join results while validating release authority at commit. Whether the cost of that validation and any related cache work still permits median overhead below 15% has to be measured or otherwise established; the hypothesis supplies no overhead result.
What does “median overhead below 15%” compare against?

It refers to median workflow latency overhead relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement. “Below” is strict: a measured median overhead of exactly 15% would not satisfy the stated target. It is not a promise that each individual workflow incurs less than 15% overhead.
If the median is below 15%, can a rare revoked release be accepted as a trade-off?

No. The hypothesis requires *both* elimination of revoked releases and median overhead below 15%. Favorable performance cannot turn a release based on revoked authority into a tenant-authorized declassification.
If no revoked releases are observed in a test, does that establish the first part of the hypothesis?

It would be an observation for the tested cases, not automatically a guarantee across every cache, revocation, release-commit, and retry interleaving. The claim that revoked releases are eliminated requires an argument appropriate to that scope. This hypothesis itself reports no test result or proof.
Does eliminating revoked releases automatically establish low-trace noninterference?

No. It addresses one important authorization route, but low-visible outputs could also be affected through other cache or retry interactions. The broader information-flow goal covers concurrent execution and retries except for tenant-authorized declassification. This hypothesis predicts a particular release safeguard and performance outcome, not a complete proof of every low-trace property.
What is the most careful concise wording for the hypothesis?

Tenant-local epoch-keyed label joins, combined with atomic revocation-epoch validation when a release commits, are hypothesized to prevent releases based on revoked authority while keeping median workflow latency overhead strictly below 15% relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement. Both predictions remain to be established.
Let’s add atomic epoch checks at release commit, repeat the revocation-race tests, and compare mismatches and overhead against the partition and cached-join baselines. Can you break down that plan?

The implementation step is to add an atomic check of the relevant revocation epoch at the point a release commits. The evaluation step is to repeat the revocation-race tests with that check in place. The comparison step is to assess trace mismatches and median workflow latency overhead against both named baselines: partitions and cached joins. This is a plan for implementation and evaluation, not a report that the checks work or that either comparison has a particular outcome.
Why put the epoch check at release commit rather than only when the capability is first presented?

Authorization can matter at two different times. A capability may be examined earlier, while the disclosure happens when the release commits. A check only at the earlier point would not, by itself, establish what revocation state applies at commit. Placing the proposed check there addresses that gap without assuming that an earlier verification or cached join remains sufficient authority.
What is the role of atomicity in that check?

The intended role is to prevent a competing revocation from falling into an unaccounted-for interval between validating the epoch and committing the release. The plan calls for an atomic epoch check at commit, but it does not specify a synchronization mechanism or prove that a particular implementation achieves the intended ordering.
Does the plan say precisely which operation wins if revocation and release commit occur at the same time?

No. A correct design would need a precise rule for their ordering so that a release cannot rely on authority already revoked under that rule. This plan specifies where to add the check and that revocation races should be retested; it does not define every boundary case or its implementation.
Will the added check replace tenant-local epoch-keyed join caching?

Replacement is not what the plan says. It calls for adding atomic epoch checks at release commit and comparing the resulting behavior against a cached-join baseline, as well as a partition baseline. The commit-time check concerns release authority; caching joins concerns reuse of label computations. The plan does not say to discard join caching.
Could a cached label join still be used if the release check happens later?

Potentially, provided its reuse is appropriate to the tenant and epoch context. The important distinction is that reusing a label computation must not itself authorize a release. The proposed commit-time check is meant to assess the revocation state when disclosure occurs. The plan does not prescribe the complete rule for selecting or retaining cached joins.
What exactly do we gain by repeating the revocation-race tests?

The proposal does not claim that checking one particular tenant would establish the result for all tenants.

Stuttering simulation allows one execution to take steps that do not change the observations relevant to the tenant while the other execution takes a different number of such steps. The argument relates executions by their meaningful observable behavior rather than requiring internal actions to occur in lockstep. That is useful when cache operations and retries introduce internal steps or different interleavings that should not, by themselves, count as a change in a tenant’s visible output.

No. An internal step might change cache state or retry scheduling and later affect a tenant-visible output. Calling an eviction or retry action internal is not enough to show it cannot carry protected information to another tenant.

Concurrent executions may have different sequences of cache actions and retry steps even when they expose equivalent information. A simulation argument can relate those sequences while accounting for steps that are invisible at the chosen observation level. It would have to address interleavings where cache activity affects a retry, or a retry affects cache activity, rather than reasoning about each component only in isolation. Does “across cache/retry interleavings” mean every internal schedule must be identical between the executions being compared?

No. It means the proposed argument must account for how cache operations and retries can be ordered during concurrent execution. The proposal therefore includes atomic retry/release commits so that changes associated with retried work and a release are not treated as disconnected, partially effective actions. The exact relationship among a retry, its notification, and any release must be specified in a design; the proposal does not give a transaction protocol.
What do you mean by an atomic retry/release commit?

At the conceptual level, it is a commit boundary for retry and release effects that must not expose an inconsistent intermediate state to the information-flow argument. For example, a release must not become effective on the strength of an authorization check that is disconnected from the state being committed. “Atomic” expresses the intended indivisibility of the relevant action; it does not choose a locking, messaging, or storage implementation.
Are you saying every retry must itself release protected information?

No. Retries can occur without a release. The proposal addresses how retry and release commits behave when they interact; it does not turn retrying into authorization to declassify. A release remains an exception only when the tenant explicitly authorizes it.
Could an atomic commit alone make a release authorized?

No. Atomicity concerns when the operation takes effect and how its parts are kept together. Authorization concerns whether the tenant permitted the disclosure, including its applicable scope. An atomically committed unauthorized release would still be unauthorized. The proposal needs those concepts to remain distinct.
How might a retry affect a notification even if no release occurs?

Conceptually, a retried action could change which notification is pending or when a notification becomes visible. If that difference depends on another tenant’s protected information and reaches the observing tenant’s low trace, it is relevant to isolation. The proposal does not assert that any particular retry has this behavior; it identifies the sort of interaction the outboxes and formal invariant must address.
Does making the retry/release commit atomic eliminate all scheduling channels?

Not by itself. Atomicity can constrain a particular commit boundary, but other concurrent cache, retry, or notification operations may still affect tenant-visible behavior. Establishing the intended termination-insensitive noninterference property requires reasoning across the relevant interleavings and observations, not merely naming an atomic operation.
What is the proposed TLAPS queue invariant for?

It is the formal condition intended to capture the queue property needed for the notification outboxes and low-step matching. A useful invariant would need to hold initially and remain true across relevant transitions, including retries, releases, and concurrent activity. The proposal says to use a TLAPS queue invariant; it does not give its formula or report that TLAPS has verified it.
Could the invariant simply say that each outbox has a tenant identifier?

That alone would not necessarily address whether pending low notifications can differ in a way that changes a later visible step. Tenant identifiers may be part of expressing partitioning, but an invariant adequate for the desired proof must relate the queue state to the tenant-low observations and authorized releases. The exact statement is still open.
Would the invariant need to say something about queues in paired executions?

For a proof comparing paired executions, it would need to provide whatever relation on their reachable queue states supports matching low-visible steps. That may involve their pending notifications and the authorization context of any permitted release. The proposal does not fix whether the formal condition is expressed as equality, a release-aware relation, or another precise predicate.
Why mention reachability when discussing a queue invariant?

An invariant must be established for states reached from its specified initial conditions and preserved by the modeled transitions. A relation that looks reasonable for one pair of queues is not enough if the transition system can later leave it. Likewise, excluding a troublesome queue state requires an argument based on the model, not merely a declaration that the state is unreachable. This proposal contains no such completed argument.
Can TLAPS verify the queue invariant without modeling the retry and release steps that modify the outbox?

A meaningful preservation check would have to include the modeled steps that can affect the invariant. If retries or releases modify the relevant queue state, leaving those effects out would narrow what a verification establishes. The proposal does not supply the model or the TLAPS result, so the exact obligations remain to be formulated.
Would a verified queue invariant by itself prove the entire information-flow property?

Not automatically. It could support the low-step-matching and notification parts of a release-aware proof, but the full termination-insensitive noninterference claim also depends on the observation model, shared-cache behavior, retries, and valid tenant-authorized declassification. A queue invariant needs to be connected to those proof obligations; the proposal does not claim that connection is already established.
How should the outbox and the formal relation handle an authorized release that legitimately changes a low notification?

The comparison should allow precisely the difference that the tenant authorized, while continuing to constrain other pending notifications and later outputs. A release must not turn an entire outbox into an unrestricted exception. The proposal calls for release-aware isolation, but it does not define a particular release-normalization rule for notification queues.
And if a release capability has been revoked?

Then a disclosure cannot be treated as tenant-authorized merely because that capability existed earlier. Atomic retry/release commits and the formal queue reasoning must respect the applicable authorization at the release boundary. The proposal does not specify the revocation protocol or report a result for any revocation race.
What exactly is the 15% median-overhead CI gate?

It is a proposed continuous-integration check against the runtime’s performance requirement: median workflow latency overhead must stay below 15% compared with identical executions without information-flow enforcement. The gate is intended to flag a candidate that fails that threshold. It does not itself measure an overhead here, specify a benchmark workload, or guarantee that every individual workflow has less than 15% overhead.
Does a median overhead of exactly 15% pass that gate?

It should not pass if the gate enforces the stated goal faithfully. The goal says *below* 15%, which is a strict comparison; exactly 15% is not below it. The proposal does not provide an observed median or define measurement tolerances.
Does ‘15% median-overhead CI gate’ mean median latency must be less than 15 milliseconds?

No. The unit is percent overhead, not milliseconds of latency. The comparison is median workflow latency overhead versus identical executions without information-flow enforcement. The proposal does not specify an absolute latency limit.
If a change passes the CI gate, can we assume the queue invariant holds?

No. The gate checks a performance criterion; TLAPS verification addresses a formal security obligation. A median overhead below 15% does not prove notification isolation, and a verified queue invariant would not measure median workflow latency. Both sides must retain their separate meaning.
Could we avoid a gate failure by disabling outbox partitioning or the atomic commits?

That would not demonstrate that the proposed enforced runtime meets both requirements. The latency comparison is for executions with information-flow enforcement against identical executions without it. Removing a proposed isolation control solely to lower the number would leave the security claim to be re-established for the resulting design. The proposal does not authorize that trade-off.

No. A CI gate can enforce the threshold on the executions it measures under its configured comparison, but it does not automatically guarantee the median for every workload or environment. The proposal names the gate and threshold without stating how its workload is chosen or reporting any pass.
Do these four proposed elements amount to a completed deployment plan?

No. They are a design proposal: tenant-partitioned notification outboxes, atomic retry/release commits, a TLAPS queue invariant, and a 15% median-overhead CI gate. The proposal does not announce an implementation result, TLAPS verification, measured overhead, or deployment decision.
Can you restate the proposal in a way that keeps the security and performance obligations explicit?

Propose tenant-partitioned notification outboxes and atomic retry/release commits to constrain low-visible effects under concurrent execution; specify and verify a TLAPS queue invariant to support release-aware information-flow reasoning; and add a CI gate requiring median workflow latency overhead strictly below 15% versus identical executions without information-flow enforcement. The proposal does not claim that isolation has been proved or that the gate has been passed.
Does atomic outbox insertion preserve pending-notification equality through crashes and replayed retries without exceeding 15% median latency overhead?

The latency side asks whether the resulting enforcement remains within the median-overhead bound; no crash/replay finding or overhead measurement is stated here.
What does pending-notification equality compare in that question?

It concerns the pending low notifications in the relevant outboxes of paired executions, as needed to match what a tenant could observe next. It is not a requirement that every tenant have the same notifications as every other tenant, nor that the two executions have identical internal states. The exact equality needed in the presence of authorized releases would have to be defined.
Why might atomic insertion be relevant if the notifications are still pending?

Because a pending notification can later become a tenant-visible output. An insertion that crosses a crash boundary may affect whether that notification is present when a retry proceeds. Atomicity is proposed as a way of making the insertion take effect coherently, but whether that yields equal pending low notifications across paired executions remains to be shown.
Does an atomic insertion guarantee the notification appears once and only once after a crash?

Not by the word “atomic” alone. Atomicity concerns the insertion taking effect as a unit; replayed retries raise a separate question about repeated attempts and their effects. If both sides of a paired execution insert a notification atomically, is equality automatic?

No. Atomicity of each insertion does not establish that the two sides insert corresponding low notifications, or that a crash and retry leave both outboxes related afterward. The proof obligation is about the paired states under the allowed interleavings, not just the integrity of each individual insertion.

Do we have to specify what survives the crash before testing equality?

Yes, to make the question precise. The result depends on which pending outbox state and retry state the model retains across a crash and what can be replayed afterward. The current question does not supply those semantics; it asks whether atomic insertion can preserve equality under them rather than reporting an established answer.
Why call out replayed retries rather than retries in general?

Replay after a crash makes repeated processing particularly relevant. An insertion could have taken effect before the crash even though the retried work later revisits the action. The question asks whether pending-notification equality survives that combination, not merely whether an ordinary retry preserves it when no crash intervenes.
Is a repeated insertion necessarily a low-trace mismatch?

Not necessarily. It depends on whether it changes the pending low-notification relation and ultimately the low observations under comparison. A duplicate could be relevant to equality even before delivery, but the question does not state that a duplicate occurs or define how repeated insertions are handled. We should examine rather than assume the outcome.
Could both executions acquire identical duplicates and still satisfy pending-notification equality?

They might satisfy a literal equality condition at that moment, depending on its definition. But matching duplicates alone would not establish that retry behavior, release authorization, and subsequent low traces are correct. The immediate question is whether atomic insertion maintains the intended paired relation through crashes and replays, not whether equality in one snapshot proves the whole information-flow property.
How do authorized releases affect equality of pending notifications?

A tenant-authorized release may permit a particular observable difference between protected-input variants. The relation must account for that permitted difference without excusing unrelated pending notifications. The question does not say whether the equality is literal for all pending notifications or is formulated after accounting for authorized release effects; that distinction matters when assessing it.
Could an authorized release make any post-crash notification difference acceptable?

No. Authorization applies to the disclosure within its scope, not every difference following a crash or retry. If a replay changes a pending low notification outside that scope, it still belongs in the isolation analysis. Atomic insertion does not broaden what the tenant authorized.
What if the capability behind a release was revoked before the replay?

A disclosure relying on revoked authority should not be treated as an authorized exception merely because an earlier attempt or outbox insertion was associated with the capability. To reason about that case, the crash, replay, authorization, and release-commit semantics would need to be specified together. This question does not report an outcome for revocation during a replay.
Does atomic outbox insertion include atomic capability consumption?

Not necessarily. Insertion into an outbox and exercising release authority are distinguishable actions unless a design explicitly relates their commit points. The question names atomic outbox insertion; it does not define which other operations share that atomic boundary. It would be an unsupported assumption to treat insertion alone as proof that a release was validly consumed.
Is the question asking whether the outbox implementation is crash-proof in every sense?

No. Its specific concern is preserving pending-notification equality through crashes and replayed retries, while meeting the median latency condition. It does not assert a general guarantee against every consequence of a crash, nor define all operational recovery requirements.
What would a careful paired-execution check look for conceptually?

Start with paired states related for a chosen tenant, allow protected information to differ, and consider a crash and replayed retry on either relevant execution. At each modeled step, ask whether the resulting pending low notifications remain related and whether any eventual observable difference falls strictly within a tenant-authorized release. That outlines the question to check, not a completed model or proof.
Must the crashes occur at the same instant in the two paired executions?

Assuming identical crash positions would narrow the claim and would need to be stated rather than inferred.
Would a test with no notification mismatch after some replayed retries settle the unbounded-retry proof?

This node neither specifies such a test result nor claims that proof.
How does the latency condition apply to atomic insertion?

Any overhead figure would need comparison with identical executions without information-flow enforcement.
Does “without exceeding 15%” allow a measured median of exactly 15%?

Taken literally, “not exceeding 15%” includes exactly 15%. If the median were below 15%, would that prove pending-notification equality?

No. Latency and the formal equality condition are distinct. And if pending notifications stayed equal, would that establish the latency bound?

Would tenant-partitioned outboxes by themselves answer that concern?

Atomic insertion and the relevant retry semantics still need to be assessed together.
What is the concise, careful formulation of the open question?

Can atomic insertion into tenant-partitioned notification outboxes maintain the appropriate paired equality of pending low notifications through crashes and replayed retries, accounting only for tenant-authorized releases, while keeping median workflow latency overhead strictly below 15% against identical executions without information-flow enforcement? Neither the preservation claim nor the overhead result is established here.

Here’s the hypothesis: atomic retry/release commits to tenant-partitioned outboxes with retry-ID deduplication preserve pending-notification equality after crashes below 15% median overhead. How should I interpret the whole claim?

It predicts two outcomes for the proposed combination. On the isolation side, paired executions should retain the required equality of pending low notifications after crashes, even when retried work is replayed. On the performance side, median workflow latency overhead should remain strictly below 15% relative to identical executions without information-flow enforcement. Atomic retry/release commits, tenant-partitioned outboxes, and retry-ID deduplication are the proposed means; neither outcome is reported as proved or measured here.
What does each of those three mechanisms contribute conceptually?

Tenant-partitioned outboxes distinguish which tenant’s pending notifications are being managed. Does tenant-partitioned mean the paired executions have to contain identical outboxes for every tenant?

Why does the hypothesis say atomic retry/release commits rather than atomic notification insertion alone?

It places the proposed atomic boundary around the retry/release commit, which is broader wording than a guarantee about one isolated insertion. It does not specify which writes, checks, or queue operations share that boundary; those details cannot be inferred from the phrase.
Does every retry in this design include a declassification release?

No. The phrase addresses commits where retry and release behavior interact; it does not imply that all retries declassify information. A release still requires tenant authorization. The hypothesis does not set a rule that turns a retry into a release or grants permission to disclose solely because work was retried.
If the commit is atomic, does that alone guarantee that replay cannot duplicate a notification?

No. Atomicity concerns an operation taking effect as a coherent unit. Replaying that coherent operation is a separate issue: without effective deduplication, it might be applied again. What is the retry ID identifying?

In this hypothesis, the retry ID is the proposed basis for recognizing a repeated retry when deduplicating its effects. Could retry-ID deduplication be treated as a substitute for release-capability authorization?

No. Deduplication asks whether the same retry is being processed again; authorization asks whether a particular disclosure is permitted. What role does a crash play in the predicted equality?

Does stuttering permit the two executions to take different numbers of recovery and retry steps?

Is the aim that no outbox ever has a duplicate entry, even internally?

What if the first attempt never committed?

Does tenant partitioning stop cross-tenant cache interference as well?

How should the predicted equality handle an explicitly authorized release that changes what a tenant may see?

The isolation goal permits differences within tenant-authorized declassification. Could a retried release be accepted just because it was authorized before the crash?

Would finding matching outboxes after one crash-and-replay test prove it for unbounded retries?

What exactly is the latency requirement attached to this hypothesis?

I propose enforcing proof-to-code conformance with transition-level runtime assertions, tenant-isolated audit logs, and a sub-15% median-overhead deployment gate. How do those three pieces fit together?

They address the gap between a formal account of information-flow isolation and the behavior of an implemented multi-tenant workflow runtime. Transition-level runtime assertions would check selected obligations where the implementation takes relevant steps. Tenant-isolated audit logs would make events reviewable without making the audit mechanism itself a cross-tenant disclosure path. The deployment gate would keep the performance requirement explicit: median workflow latency overhead must be below 15% versus identical executions without information-flow enforcement. This is a proposal, not a claim that conformance has already been established or that the gate has passed.
What does “proof-to-code conformance” mean here?

It means checking that the code’s relevant behavior corresponds to the transitions and constraints relied on by the proof. A proof about a model does not automatically cover an implementation whose cache, retry, release, or notification behavior differs from that model. The proposal calls for mechanisms to enforce that connection, but does not specify a complete refinement map or claim that one has been verified.
Why make the runtime assertions transition-level?

A transition-level assertion checks a relevant condition as an operation changes runtime state, rather than examining only an eventual output. That is potentially useful where a retry, cache action, or release changes the state on which the information-flow argument depends. The proposal does not specify which transitions carry assertions, their exact predicates, or whether checking them alone covers every behavior in the proof.
Are these assertions supposed to reproduce the entire formal proof while the workflow runs?

No. Runtime assertions can check conditions at particular transitions, but a collection of checks is not automatically a full proof of termination-insensitive noninterference under concurrent execution and retries. Proof-to-code conformance also requires an argument that the checks, the implemented transitions, and the formal model correspond in the ways the security claim needs. The proposal does not state that the whole proof is executed at runtime.
Can you give a general illustration of the difference between checking a transition and checking only a final output?

As a general illustration, a final workflow result might look acceptable even though an intermediate retry or release transition failed to maintain a condition on which later isolation depends. A transition-level assertion is aimed at detecting the condition when that state change happens. This illustrates the proposed role of assertions; it does not assert that any particular transition has failed or prescribe a specific assertion.
Would an assertion that never fires prove that the code conforms?

Not on its own. It matters whether the assertion expresses the right condition, is placed on all relevant paths, and actually observes the state required for that condition. Absence of a reported violation is not proof that unasserted behavior matches the model. The proposal is to use transition-level assertions as part of enforcing conformance, not to treat their silence as an unrestricted guarantee.
How does concurrency affect that conformance question?

Concurrent operations can interleave in ways that change what a transition sees or leaves behind. If the formal argument relies on a particular relationship between steps, the implementation’s asserted conditions need to remain meaningful across those interleavings. An assertion that checks an isolated operation without accounting for relevant concurrent behavior might miss the very state change the information-flow claim depends on. The proposal does not define an assertion strategy for every interleaving.
Could assertions be restricted to declassification, since that is the explicit exception?

The proposal does not impose that restriction. Explicitly authorized declassification is an important boundary, but the overall isolation goal also concerns shared caches and asynchronous retries. Which transitions need runtime checks depends on the claimed proof-to-code correspondence. Checking releases alone would not, merely by its name, establish correspondence for other modeled behavior.
Would transition-level assertions themselves authorize a release?

No. An assertion can test a condition; it cannot create tenant authorization. A disclosure remains an allowed exception only if the tenant explicitly authorized it within the applicable scope. Passing an assertion must not be mistaken for permission beyond that authorization.
What is the purpose of tenant-isolated audit logs?

They provide an auditable record while maintaining tenant isolation in the audit path itself. In a multi-tenant runtime, a log can contain information about a tenant’s workflows or releases; making it tenant-isolated is intended to prevent another tenant from learning protected information simply through audit access. The proposal does not define log entries, retention, storage, or access-control machinery.
Are those logs meant to contain every internal cache and retry step?

The proposal does not say which events the logs contain. Calling them tenant-isolated audit logs establishes their intended isolation and audit role, not a requirement to record every internal action. Their scope would need to be defined before claiming that a particular behavior is auditable.
Could a log of a declassification be treated as the authorization for that declassification?

No. An audit record and an authorization are distinct. Recording that a release occurred does not make the release tenant-authorized. Likewise, the record itself must not disclose protected information to an audience outside its permitted scope merely because it resides in an audit log.
What would make an audit log tenant-isolated if the underlying runtime is shared?

The intended property is that one tenant’s audit information cannot become another tenant’s unauthorized observation through the shared system. That concerns both what may be recorded and who may observe it. The proposal names the required separation but does not choose a physical storage arrangement, keying scheme, or access protocol.
Does tenant-isolated mean an authorized release cannot be audited across a tenant boundary?

Not as a blanket rule. Explicitly tenant-authorized declassification can permit a disclosure within its scope, while the audit mechanism must still respect the authorization and tenant isolation for everything else. The proposal does not define who may review a particular record or what an authorized release permits an audit entry to reveal.

The decision sets elimination as the condition for lifting this deployment block. Merely lowering the frequency of unauthorized receipt differences would not satisfy that wording. The decision does not specify a particular test, proof method, or numerical criterion for establishing elimination.
Would changing the acknowledgment implementation be enough to lift the block?

Not simply because it has been changed. The condition is that tenant-local audit acknowledgments eliminate the receipt leaks. An implementation change is a proposed means; its effect on tenant-visible receipts must be established before describing this condition as met.
If the workflow latency overhead remains acceptable, can deployment proceed while the receipts still leak?

No. This decision explicitly blocks deployment until the receipt leaks are eliminated through tenant-local audit acknowledgments. A favorable performance result would not make an unauthorized cross-tenant observation permissible.
Does this decision provide a new latency measurement or change the median-overhead goal?

No. It states which design measures to retain and the condition blocking deployment. It reports no new latency measurement and does not alter the separate median workflow latency overhead requirement.
Are epoch-checked releases supposed to fix the audit acknowledgments too?

The decision does not claim that. Epoch-checked releases concern whether release authority is valid when exercised. Tenant-local audit acknowledgments address whether the auditing path exposes protected cross-tenant activity through receipts. Validating a release does not automatically constrain every observation made possible by its audit acknowledgment.
Could atomic outboxes be considered a substitute for tenant-local audit acknowledgments?

No substitution is stated. The decision keeps atomic outboxes and separately requires tenant-local audit acknowledgments to eliminate receipt leaks. Atomicity at an outbox commit does not, by itself, answer what a tenant-visible audit receipt reveals.
Does the decision require turning off audit receipts altogether?
No. It calls for tenant-local audit acknowledgments that eliminate receipt leaks, not for removing acknowledgments. It does not choose a particular way to achieve that condition.
What if we simply stop showing receipts to tenants?

The decision does not select that approach. Its stated condition is to use tenant-local audit acknowledgments and eliminate receipt leaks. Whether a different receipt policy would meet the design’s broader requirements is not decided here.
Are we blocking only the audit feature, or deployment of the runtime?
The decision says to block deployment. It does not limit the block to the audit feature while allowing the runtime to deploy with the identified receipt issue unresolved.
Does “until” mean deployment automatically happens as soon as someone says the acknowledgments are tenant-local?

No. The condition concerns eliminating receipt leaks, not merely naming the acknowledgments tenant-local. The decision also does not state that deployment happens automatically once this particular condition is satisfied or settle any other deployment requirements.
Could a receipt leak remain even if no unauthorized release is committed?

Yes, conceptually. A receipt could expose information about another tenant’s release activity without itself being an unauthorized declassification commit. That is why the decision treats the audit-acknowledgment path as a separate deployment concern rather than assuming release checks alone settle it.
Does the decision declare the retained components insecure?

No. It retains partitioned caches, epoch-checked releases, and atomic outboxes. The stated deployment obstacle is receipt leakage through audit acknowledgments. The decision does not make a broader judgment about every property of the retained components.
What should we avoid claiming about a fix at this point?

Avoid claiming that tenant-local acknowledgments have already been implemented, that receipt leaks have been eliminated, or that deployment is approved. The decision identifies the required direction and blocks deployment until the condition is met; it supplies no result showing that it has been met.
Give me a concise statement of the decision.
Retain partitioned caches, epoch-checked releases, and atomic outboxes, but block deployment until tenant-local audit acknowledgments eliminate the receipt leaks.
